correctness.rationale: An independent set uses at most one vertex per position, and two omitted colors would be indistinguishable in each clique. For vertices at i,j, distance equality at a landmark (t,a) fixes |i−t|−|j−t| to 0 or ±1 as dictated by its color; the left side has constant parity and is monotone in t. For q>=4 an injection of q−1 colors has both a matching and a neutral landmark for every pair of different colors and hence resolves by parity. Equal colors are resolved by two distinct landmark positions. For q=3 the two-landmark candidate with different colors a,b at s<t fails on (s+1,a) and (s,b). Three distinct colors resolve as before. An alternating triple a,b,a rules out a collision of a and b by monotonicity; pairs involving the omitted color have a matching and neutral landmark. Nonalternating two-color triples have a cut at s, the last position of the earlier color a, and the same collision (s+1,a),(s,b) works on both entire sides. With q=2, a single landmark has two neighbors, different-color pairs fail by the cut collision, and same-color pairs not covering both endpoints fail on the site just beyond an extreme versus the other color at that extreme. At the endpoints the path difference has opposite signs, so same-color endpoint pairs resolve and are independent exactly for L>=3. These characterize the labeled bases and give the claimed counts, including the short-path impossibilities from the projection cap. My independent finite check compared actual basis sets, not just their counts, on 11 graphs; replay `python3 /workspace/review_evidence/check_4.py`. The proof, not the finite range, establishes the universal result.

evidence: The projection lemma applies to ordinary resolving sets, and gives the q−1 color lower bound; the section on complete graph–path products states the ordinary q−1 dimension for q>=3.
The founding article's abstract discusses ir=1,n−1,n−2 and realization results for general graphs.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Projection alone only checks pairs in a common clique, not cross-position collisions or the q=3 penalty. The two independent-resolving articles were not ruled out on the basis of excerpts.

evidence: Independence caps the number of landmarks at L, so projection already implies a portion of the short-path boundary. The inspected theorem gives only the ordinary dimension, and the indexed independent-resolving excerpt supplies no usable complete classification.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: That lower bound does not imply the endpoint restriction at q=2, the extra landmark and alternating-color bases at q=3, or sufficiency of all minimum injections at q>=4. Those depend on the parity and cut-collision analysis.

value.rationale: For the standard clique–path Cartesian family, the classification explains when imposing independence destroys resolvability and identifies the exceptional three-color penalty despite a uniform ordinary dimension formula. It gives all optimal labeled configurations, including both geometrically distinct kinds at q=3, rather than merely exhibiting a construction or obtaining a few exact instances.
residual_risks: Only minimum independent resolving sets in the complete-fiber path product are classified.
